Truck Driver Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A truck driver resume has to prove one thing above all: that you can run freight on time, keep the load and the rig safe, and bring the truck back clean. Hiring managers do not hire on a list of trucks. They hire on licence class, route range, and a record of on-time deliveries with a clean safety record.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, the skills hiring sides scan for, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

Quick answer: A truck driver resume should open with your CDL class and driving record, name the routes, freight, and mileage you handled, show on-time delivery and safety records, list your endorsements and certifications, and prove reliability over real miles — then keep the layout single-column with standard headings so tracking systems parse every section cleanly.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with your CDL class and driving record — what you are licensed to drive, and where.
  • Prove reliability with on-time delivery kept, detention cut, and miles driven safely.
  • Name the routes, freight, and scale from the posting.
  • Every bullet pairs a task with a result: what you hauled, where, and what changed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Trucking Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a fleet manager and you will not hear "passionate about driving." You will hear:

  • CDL class and driving record. A clean licence, the right class for the rig, and no preventable accidents — checked before anything else.
  • Route range and freight types. Long-haul, regional, dedicated, and local runs, with dry van, refrigerated, flatbed, and tanker freight — name the routes and loads you actually hauled.
  • On-time delivery kept. Freight delivered on schedule, appointments kept, and detention kept short. "125,000 miles a year, on time" is a hiring signal; "worked hard" is not.
  • Load handling and hours-of-service compliance. Securing, tarping, scaling, and logging — and keeping the electronic log clean so nothing comes back on the carrier. Careful handling beats fast driving.
  • Safety and vehicle care. Pre-trip inspections, fuel and defect reports, and a clean safety record. A resume with no mention of safe driving tells a hiring manager your work is a risk.

If your resume reads like a truck list — all rigs and trailers, no routes — it will lose to a freight record.

Truck Driver Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a truck driver with long-haul, regional, and refrigerated freight experience. It is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

JAMES WHITFIELD — Truck Driver
Dallas, TX · (214) 555-0183 · james.whitfield@email.com · Class A CDL · Clean Driving Record

SUMMARY
Truck driver with 8 years of long-haul and regional freight work. Ran a 2,400-mile weekly over-the-road loop for a national carrier, kept on-time delivery at 99.1% across 125,000 miles a year, and held a zero-preventable-accident record for 6 years. Dry van, refrigerated, and flatbed freight; Class A CDL with HazMat and Tanker endorsements, TWIC card, DOT medical card current.

LICENCES & CERTIFICATIONS
Class A Commercial Driving Licence · HazMat Endorsement · Tanker Endorsement · TWIC Card · DOT Medical Card · Defensive Driving Course · OSHA Forklift Operator Certification

SKILLS
Long-haul route driving · Regional & dedicated routes · Refrigerated transport · Flatbed load securement · Electronic logging (ELD) · Hours-of-service compliance · Pre-trip inspections · Route planning & GPS navigation · Load scaling & weight distribution · Customer service · Detention management · Fuel-efficient driving · Warehouse loading & unloading

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

OTR Truck Driver — LoneStar Freight Lines, Dallas, TX | 2020–Present - Ran a 2,400-mile weekly over-the-road loop, finishing on schedule with 99.1% on-time delivery across 125,000 miles a year - Cut detention time by 35% with a pre-arrival call routine, saving 90 waiting hours in one year - Improved fuel efficiency from 6.8 to 7.4 miles per gallon with steady-speed driving and idle-time discipline - Held a zero-preventable-accident record for 6 years and 2.1 million career miles, with clean roadside inspections throughout - Mentored 4 new drivers; three of my trainees passed their route assessments on the first attempt

Regional Truck Driver — RedRiver Logistics, Fort Worth, TX | 2018–2020 - Ran 5-state regional routes with 600-mile days, keeping every refrigerated load inside its temperature window - Hauled 40 chilled loads a week to grocery distribution centres, with zero spoilage claims across two years - Read load sheets and marked up delivery windows, catching 6 timing clashes before the road - Covered the lead driver's holidays, running the full regional round end to end with no missed appointments

Local Delivery Driver — MetroHaul Transport, Dallas, TX | 2016–2018 - Worked same-day freight runs across the metro area, learning the pace of a real delivery schedule - Collected and delivered 45 loads a day on a tight downtown loop, with a zero-missed-pickup record in the final year - Earned promotion to regional driver after completing the induction and passing the driving assessment

EDUCATION
High School Diploma — Skyline High School, Dallas, TX, 2016 Commercial Driver Training — Dallas CDL Academy, 2016 Defensive Driving Course — National Safety Council, 2021

Why it works: the summary leads with the two things trucking hiring managers check first — CDL class and a freight record kept on time (125,000 miles, 99.1% on-time, 2.1 million career miles) — then names the freight. Every bullet pairs a task with a result.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: licence, scope, delivery record

"Class A CDL," "2,400-mile weekly loop," "99.1% on-time delivery," "125,000 miles a year" — four facts that place you in thirty seconds. Lead with licence and a result, not training.

Experience: jobs with outcomes, not duties

"Drove a truck for a carrier" is a duty; "cut detention time by 35% while holding the delivery schedule" is proof. Miles per year, on-time rates, fuel saved, and accidents avoided are the metrics that matter.

Routes and freight: proof you can haul the trade

Your range is the closest thing to proof a truck driver gets. Name the routes you actually drove — long-haul loops, regional rounds, refrigerated runs — and the freight behind them. List only work you could do tomorrow.

Skills: mirror the posting, honestly

List the freight and tools you have actually worked with, in the posting's own words — "long-haul route driving" versus "driving work" matters to filters, as does "hours-of-service compliance" versus "following rules." Depth in one part of the trade beats a long list.

Truck Driver Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "long-haul route driving" vs "driving work" matters to filters:

  • Driving: long-haul route driving, regional routes, dedicated routes, local runs, refrigerated transport, flatbed hauling, dry van freight, tanker runs
  • Freight types: dry van, refrigerated freight, flatbed loads, tanker freight, HazMat loads, grocery distribution, retail restocking
  • Safety & compliance: clean driving record, defensive driving, pre-trip inspections, defect reporting, load securement, hours-of-service compliance, ELD logs, inspection readiness
  • Tools & reading: route planning, GPS navigation, electronic logging, load sheets, bills of lading, proof of delivery, detention management, fuel-efficient driving

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Trucking companies screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. 5 Mistakes That Cost Truck Drivers Interviews

  1. A truck list, not a freight record. A long list of rigs with no routes, miles, or loads reads as a hobbyist. Add numbers that show you finished it.
  2. Hiding the CDL class. If your CDL class and driving record are buried at the bottom, a hiring manager may never reach them. Put licence in the summary and header.
  3. Duties without results. "Drove a truck across the country" could describe anyone with a licence. Add the result — shorter detention, better fuel use, a driver trained — to every bullet.
  4. Vague route claims. List what you hauled, route after route.
  5. Ignoring safety and inspections. A resume with no mention of pre-trip inspections, defect reports, or a clean safety record tells a hiring manager your work is a risk. Put safety up front.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a CDL to work as a truck driver?

Yes, for anything over the standard licence weight limit. A Class A CDL covers tractor-trailers and the heaviest rigs, while a Class B covers straight trucks and box trucks. Check the posting for the vehicle class, and list your exact CDL class at the top of your resume so the hiring manager sees it first.

What experience should a new truck driver put on a resume?

Lead with jobs and scope. A local delivery run on a busy metro loop, a warehouse loading shift, or a driving-school placement all count. Name what you hauled, how many miles, and what changed — the same pattern as a senior bullet.

How do I show on-time delivery and reliability on a truck driver resume?

Name the record: miles per year, on-time rates kept, and accidents avoided — detention cut, fuel saved, inspections passed. "125,000 miles a year with 99.1% on-time delivery" tells a manager more than any adjective.

Should a truck driver resume include photos of my truck or work?

No — keep the resume itself text-only so tracking systems can parse it, and put truck or route photos in a separate portfolio or social profile linked from the header. A photo inside the resume file is usually stripped or misread by the parser.

How long should a truck driver resume be?

One page for most truck drivers, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across different work — long-haul, regional, refrigerated freight — and even then keep your best numbers on page one.

Do I need to list every job I have ever held as a truck driver?

No. List the jobs that show your route range and your most recent work — usually the last 10 to 15 years, including your first local delivery or warehouse role if it is your foundation. Older short roles can be dropped, but keep the timeline honest: a gap with no explanation raises more questions than a short role ever will.
